verdict.reasoning: Patient states: "I've been feeling really anxious over the past few months."

Patient reports onset: "maybe about two months or so, I've been feeling like this, and that probably coincides with, me starting a new job" and describes job: "I work for a... fashion retailer, in... the head office team... my boss is not very nice to me" and "I just really dread, going there."

Transcript includes: morning anxiety/reluctance to leave house ("I just get really nervous every morning about leaving the house"), palpitations for a few to ~10 minutes ("couple of minutes... ten minutes"), sleep-onset insomnia with 3–4 hours ("I can't get to sleep for hours... maybe, three, four hours, I'm getting now"), early waking with racing heart ("I find myself waking up before [the alarm], 'cause... my heart is racing"), daytime fatigue and anhedonia ("really, really low... I find no enjoyment at all"), decreased socializing and hobbies (avoiding friends; no longer enjoying running/tennis). She does not say she has completely stopped running/tennis, only "not going out to do that quite so much," so “cessation” overstates it, but most elements are directly supported.
When asked about panic attacks, patient says: "No I wouldn't say so" and later: "I'm just worried it's building up to that."

Low mood: "I'm pretty much, down like, I don't enjoy... my day at all" and "constant, feeling of just being a bit, down, a bit unhappy." Denies suicidal ideation: "I haven't had any suicidal thoughts or any, thoughts that have been that extreme."
Appetite: "Probably, not, significant changes maybe. No I wouldn't say that... I'm eating like, much differently. Ohh that, I probably have more chocolate than normal, just because I feel, so down."
No prior similar episodes: "Before this did you have any similar times... ?" Patient: "Not really I, I'm, no, I would say... I've never felt, anything this bad before."
"I talk to my mum, because she also suffers from, well she's, suffered from like depression in the past."
The transcript does not discuss any current medications at all; absence of mention does not confirm "no medications reported."
Living situation: "I live with my parents, just my parents." Support: "I have a good support system, like I do have good family and stuff."

Alcohol: patient says "probably quite a lot on the Friday or Saturday... I probably go over my limit just on those days" and "maybe a glass of wine during the week" and "I guess I don't really keep track of it that much," matching heavy weekend use and uncounted units.
"I try not to smoke, but I do, occasionally, but I don't take drugs." This supports occasional smoking and no illicit drug use.
The transcript does not contain an explicit diagnostic label such as work-related anxiety disorder or generalized anxiety disorder; this is a clinical interpretation, not stated in the consultation.

Doctor says palpitations are "most likely... associated with anxiety" and recommends "couple of basic blood tests" but does not specify thyroid or anemia or list test types; naming specific organic causes is additional.

Doctor: "you can self-refer via the NHS, for what we call like, talking therapy..." and "I can send you the link for that." This aligns with providing a self-referral link to NHS talking therapy (CBT-type).

Doctor: "There are some online resources that are really helpful. Um, can put the details, on there" and "I'll put some more information on your notes about, helping with your, sleep patterns and things like that," consistent with online anxiety resources and sleep hygiene advice.
Doctor: "it's probably worth having couple of basic blood tests" but does not specify FBC, TFT, U&E; naming specific panels is additional detail.
Doctor: "arranging a GP follow-up a week after you've had the tests, so we can just go through the results with you."

Doctor: "if you're feeling like it's not helping at all, or your anxiety is getting worse, to the point where you can't cope with work, or you can't, just do your normal things day-to-day. Then, it's important for... you to give us a call, back and just discuss that, further."

Doctor: "some people, with anxiety they, do need to take medication to control that but that's, not something that we'd suggest in the first instance"—this acknowledges possible future pharmacotherapy if non-pharmacologic measures are insufficient.
